Hungary is entering its "most critical 5 days" as dropping water levels on the Danube River threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant amid an extreme heatwave, Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, warning that the plant could be shut down for more than a month. (Photo by David Balogh/Xinhua) BUDAPEST, Aug. 2 (Xinhua) -- Hungary is entering its "most critical 5 days" as dropping water levels on the Danube River threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant amid an extreme heatwave, Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, warning that the plant could be shut down for more than a month. Speaking to local commercial television channel RTL, Magyar said the last remaining operating turbine at the 2,000 MW facility will likely be shut down late Sunday or on Monday. A complete halt to power generation at Paks, which accounts for nearly half of Hungary's domestic electricity generation,would mark the first full closure in the plant's 44-year history. Magyar explained earlier on social media that strict nuclear safety regulations mandate the shutdown because of record-low river levels needed for cooling water. He reassured the public that nuclear safety remains fully guaranteed, with around 50 water management experts assisting plant personnel to maintain cooling operations. The unprecedented energy crisis comes as Hungary braces for temperatures reaching 40 degrees Celsius or higher over these "most critical five days," placing immense strain on the national grid. The Hungarian government has introduced emergency measures to maintain grid stability. Under a decree that took effect on Saturday, mandatory consumption cutbacks can be enforced on major industrial consumers if necessary. However, Magyar noted that voluntary conservation efforts by businesses and the public have so far helped avoid enforced rationing. Major companies, including MOL, Audi, and Gedeon Richter, have pledged significant demand reductions. Nearly 300 companies have already pledged voluntary reductions for Monday, along with numerous state-owned firms, most local councils, civil society groups and churches, he said. To save power, decorative lighting on Budapest's iconic landmarks, including the Hungarian Parliament, Buda Castle, and the Chain Bridge, was turned off on Sunday evening. Additional measures include halting most rail freight transport between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. starting Monday, bringing reserve power units on standby, and maximizing electricity imports. "If Hungary can get through these most critical five days, temperatures are expected to drop by 5 to 7 degrees Celsius," Magyar said, adding that household restrictions remain an absolute last resort to maintain system stability. ■ An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 2, 2026 shows a view of the Paks nuclear power plant near Dunaszentbenedek, Hungary. http://en.people.cn/n3/2026/0808/c90000-.text: Home Opinion PD Voice Politics Foreign Affairs Business World We Are China Society Culture Sci-Tech Video Photo Sports Travel Military Life Exclusive Specials Languages Chinese Japanese French Spanish Russian Arabic Korean German Portuguese Swahili Italian Kazakh Thai Malay Greek Vietnamese Urdu Hindi Archive Xiplomacy: Warmth that transcends borders Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin visit a photo exhibition that celebrates the everlasting friendship between the two countries at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, May 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) BEIJING, Aug. 7 (Xinhua) -- During Russian President Vladimir Putin's China trip this May, Chinese President Xi Jinping invited him to visit a photo exhibition celebrating the everlasting friendship between the two countries at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. As the two presidents strolled through the exhibition, viewing pictures documenting their close interactions and the solid progress in China-Russia cooperation, they paused before a familiar image from Moscow's Red Square. The photograph, taken on May 9, 2025, during celebrations marking the 80th anniversary of the Soviet Union's victory in the Great Patriotic War, showed Xi seated between Putin and Russian World War II veteran Evgeny Znamensky, whose suit was adorned with medals earned through wartime service. The two leaders were seen warmly chatting with the veteran. Recalling the warm memories of their meeting in Moscow more than a year ago, the 100-year-old veteran said the temperature that day was below 10 degrees Celsius. "President Xi was concerned that I might feel cold and specifically asked for a blanket for me." Deeply touched by the gesture, Znamensky said he greatly appreciated Xi's kindness. The blanket was a small gesture, but it speaks volumes about a core tenet of China's diplomacy. "Friendship, which derives from close contact between the people, holds the key to sound state-to-state relations," Xi articulated this philosophy at the opening ceremony of the Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation in 2017. Chinese President Xi Jinping attends celebrations marking the 80th anniversary of the victory in the Soviet Union's Great Patriotic War in Moscow, Russia, May 9, 2025. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi) Throughout his overseas visits and diplomatic engagements, Xi has forged friendships with people around the world through sincerity and mutual respect. Even amid a demanding schedule, he has always made time to meet people from all walks of life. His warm smile and approachable manner have created countless memorable moments, building bridges of mutual understanding and friendship across borders. During his visit to Russia in May 2015, Xi presented commemorative badges to representatives of Russian veterans to honor their contribution to the victory of the World Anti-Fascist War. After noticing that the Russian veteran Gaverdovsky was having difficulty walking steadily, Xi told him, "I'll go over and bring the badge to you! You don't need to move." Xi then walked swiftly to Gaverdovsky, and presented the badge to him. Gaverdovsky said after the ceremony that he was deeply touched by the Chinese president's meticulous care and consideration. Chinese President Xi Jinping (C) meets with 18 representatives of Russian veterans who fought dauntlessly on the battlefield in northeast China during the anti-Japanese war and in Russia's Great Patriotic War, in Moscow, Russia, on May 8, 2015. (Xinhua/Rao Aimin) Xi is equally warm and attentive when meeting young people. In May 2024, Xi paid a state visit to Hungary. Among those greeting the Chinese leader was Hungarian girl Olah Tamara, who had presented flowers to Xi when he visited the country as Chinese vice president in 2009. After being told that she was the same girl who presented flowers to him 15 years ago, the president recalled that encounter. "You've grown up. You were only this tall back then," he said, making a gesture with his hand. The brief exchange bridged the years in an instant. Deeply moved, Olah said she had never imagined Xi would still remember her. "He is so warm and kind," she said. There are many more such moments throughout Xi's overseas visits. Greeting children in Germany on a rainy day, he reminded them to keep warm and avoid catching a cold. In Australia, he set aside time to meet primary school students who had written him letters, invited them to visit China for study tours, and encouraged them to continue writing. Visiting a high school in the U.S. state of Washington, he chatted with students about sports, music and youth. When meeting workers and farmers, Xi is known for his down-to-earth manner and genuine sincerity. Having worked and lived alongside farmers in his younger years, Xi has always shared a deep bond with them. Chinese President Xi Jinping chats with members of a local farmer's family during a visit with his wife, Peng Liyuan, in Costa Rica, June 3, 2013. (Xinhua/Zhang Duo) During a visit to a farming family in Costa Rica back in 2013, he reflected on his own experience working in China's countryside, saying he had been a farmer and personally knows what life is like for Chinese farmers. Walking through the family's small coffee plantation, Xi paused repeatedly to ask the host, Marco Tulio Zamora, about coffee cultivation, production and sales. For Zamora, the conversation was unforgettable. He said he had rarely seen a foreign leader visit an ordinary family like his, adding that his family felt deeply honored. During his visit to Serbia in 2016, Xi toured the Smederevo Steel Plant. Inside the vast and bustling hot-rolling workshop, machines roared and heat filled the air. Xi stopped from time to time, closely observing the production process and asking detailed questions about the plant's operations. Later, Xi visited the staff canteen. What interested him most was the everyday lives of the employees. Nenad Cvetanovic, a veteran employee at the Smederevo Steel Plant, still recalls the sense of encouragement among workers when the Chinese leader told them that the plant would "surely be revitalized." "President Xi's interaction with us resonated deeply among the workers at the steel plant. His care for us came straight from the heart, giving us a strong sense of security and hope," he said. Aerial photo taken on Aug. 16, 2021 shows the HBIS Serbia in Smederevo, Serbia. (HBIS Serbia/Handout via Xinhua) Established in 1913, the Smederevo Steel Plant was once regarded as "the pride of Serbia." However, by the late 1990s, declining competitiveness and weak management had pushed the plant to the brink of closure. In 2016, China's HBIS Group acquired the plant. Through joint efforts by both sides, the plant has undergone a breathtaking transformation, regaining its position as one of Serbia's key export drivers. In 2024, 30 Serbian workers from the steel mill wrote a letter to Xi, sharing the mill's development story and expressing their gratitude for his support in making the project's success possible. Xi said in his reply letter that it is a great pleasure to learn that the steel plant has turned losses into gains quickly after the investment of a Chinese-funded enterprise. The development of the plant, he said, cannot be achieved without the dedication and hard work of the workers, who have been working diligently for the quick growth of the steel plant and have written a new chapter for the iron-clad friendship between China and Serbia. "I give you a thumbs-up," Xi wrote in the letter. https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/india/.text: Three Indian nationals rescued from the Turkish-owned cargo vessel MV Royad Mammadov, which was attacked in the Black Sea on Monday, have departed for India, the Embassy of India in Bucharest has said."Three Indian nationals, Sahil Sandhu, Ashwini Kumar and Harman Singh, departed for India today (Saturday), the mission said on Saturday."The Embassy provided all necessary support and assistance to facilitate their return. We express our sincere gratitude to the Romanian authorities, Constanta County Hospital, and the Romanian rescue teams for their invaluable assistance, cooperation and support," it said.The vessel, owned by a Turkish company and carrying corn from Ukraine's Izmail port to Ravenna in Italy, was struck while sailing in the Black Sea outside Romania's territorial waters on Monday.Two foreign seafarers were killed, and several crew members were injured. All 3 Indian nationals survived, although one was injured and received medical treatment in Romania.The nationality of those killed in the attack was not immediately known.On October 7, the Embassy representative visited the three Indian nationals rescued on October 6 from the vessel in the Black Sea.Two were accommodated at a hotel, while the third is undergoing treatment at the County Hospital in Constanta. All three are in stable condition, the mission said in a post on October 7, the mission said.The Embassy facilitated essential items, including mobile phones, through the shipping company's local agent, while arranging Indian food through a local Indian restaurant, it said.The Embassy remains in close contact with the authorities concerned and continues to extend all necessary support.India has emerged as the world's second-largest supplier of seafarers, contributing 3,11,936 maritime professionals to the global shipping industry, according to the BIMCO-ICS Seafarer Workforce Report, 2026.The report estimates that India now accounts for 12.16% of the global seafaring workforce, ranking behind only the Philippines and ahead of China, the Russian Federation and Indonesia.

https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/.text: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home Taiwan News Foreign minister warns EU of China dependence dangers Reuters, WARSAW Add TT as Preferred Source Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) yesterday warned the EU that dependence on Chinese suppliers poses a risk to the bloc's freedom during a speech in Poland ahead of a summit in Brussels where trade with Beijing is to ‌be high on the agenda. EU leaders are to discuss China as the first point of their summit starting tomorrow, as Brussels attempts to reduce the bloc's trade deficit and mitigate what many see ​as the risks of becoming over-dependent on Beijing in sensitive sectors. "Because China's ​authoritarian ideology is fundamentally incompatible with Europe's democracy, dependence on China ⁠is not merely an economic risk — it's a threat to European freedom and sovereignty ​itself," Lin said in a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum. Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung speaks at the Warsaw Security Forum yesterday. Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs "A Europe controlled ​through its supply chains would be a Europe that had surrendered part of its liberty," he added. The Chinese embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to an e-mailed request for comment. Lin said that trade with Taiwan benefits Europe. "Taiwan and Europe share the values that ‌matter ⁠most: democracy, freedom, human rights and the rule of law," he said. "The Taiwan model has helped power innovation and prosperity in Silicon Valley, and it can do the same for Europe too." While foreign ministers previously only rarely visit Europe due to ​Beijing's objections, Lin has ​gone several times ⁠since he assumed his current position more than two years ago, including to Poland. Taiwan has sought closer ties with Europe, especially since ​the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. Europe has its own disputes ​with China, ⁠over both trade imbalances and also its criticism of what it sees as Chinese support for Russia.
